children.text: A stretch of white coral sand about 1–1.5 km long at the southwestern tip of Panglao Island in Bohol. By day you snorkel and dive in a sea where the coral is right off the beach, and once the sun goes down, tables are set out on the sand and the beach fills with seafood barbecue and live music.

Alona Beach is a stretch of white sand in the village of Tawala, at the southwestern tip of Panglao Island off the southwest of Bohol's main island. Because the sand is made of crushed coral, the grains are slightly coarse and pale, and the water at the shore is shallow and a clear blue-green. Both ends of the beach are closed off by leafy rocky headlands, which gives it the feel of a small, cozy bay. It is only about 1–1.5 km long, so even a leisurely stroll from end to end takes about
10–20 minutes
. It is not an endless beach like White Beach in Boracay, but that is exactly the point: everything you need is gathered in one place.
The beach is said to be named after the actress Alona Alegre, who filmed a movie scene here in the early
. With a coral sea right in front of the beach, divers began to arrive in the early
, and dive shops and small guesthouses followed, turning it into the main base for travel in Bohol. After Bohol-Panglao International Airport opened close by in
, resorts and restaurants multiplied quickly, and today it is the place in Bohol where accommodation, restaurants, tour booths and bars are packed most tightly together.
Alona Beach Road runs alongside the beach, and on both sides of it you will find resort gates, open-air restaurants, dive shops, massage stalls and money changers. In
the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) ordered the removal of buildings put up within
of the shoreline, and according to news reports about 90% of the violating structures had been removed by
October 2019

. In the bright daytime, people rest under parasols while divers head out by boat, and from sunset the restaurants put their tables out on the sand and the atmosphere changes completely. The same beach shows a completely different face by day and by night, and that is the charm of Alona.

It suits travelers who want the sea, restaurants and their lodging all within a few steps, people who want to earn a diving certification or try a taster dive, and couples and families who want to eat dinner while watching the sunset from the beach. On the other hand, if you want a quiet beach with hardly anyone on it, Alona can get crowded in peak season, so consider a calmer beach such as Doljo Beach on Panglao Island as well. Information on Panglao Island as a whole is covered separately in
Panglao

blocks.title: A walk along the beach in the early morning

children.text: Alona Beach has the fewest people around

. Outrigger boats start their engines one by one, and the shadows of the coconut palms stretch long over the sand that was washed clean by the waves overnight. At low tide the water recedes far out, and you can walk along a beach that has widened like a sandbar.

blocks.title: Snorkeling over the coral off the beach

children.text: Alona has a shallow house reef that you can enter straight from the beach without a boat, so all you need is a mask and fins to see coral and tropical fish. There are sea urchins and sharp coral on the bottom, so be sure to wear water shoes and do not step on the coral.

blocks.title: A taster dive at a dive shop

children.text: PADI dive shops line the beach, so you can try a taster dive even without a certification. According to one shop's
rate sheet, a taster dive costs about

blocks.title: Out to sea on an outrigger boat

children.text: The traditional outrigger boats lined up along the beach are your tour buses. Island-hopping tours to Balicasag Island and Virgin Island leave from the booths here, with shared tours costing about
per person and a private boat charter about
. The routes themselves are covered in detail in the Panglao entry.
The beach faces southwest, so at dusk the sky spreads with orange and red. The classic photo spot is the silhouette of outrigger boats floating on the water. Find your spot about
30 minutes
before sunset and wait for the blue hour, the ten or so minutes after the sun goes down.

blocks.title: Seafood barbecue, picked from the ice

children.text: As the sun sinks, restaurants lay out fish, shrimp, squid and shellfish on ice in front of their tables. You choose what you like, it is priced by weight and grilled over charcoal, and a meal at a beachfront restaurant usually runs around
. Checking the price list before you order keeps surprises to a minimum.
From around
restaurants and bars put their tables out onto the sand and acoustic live music starts. At peak times there are also fire-dance shows near the beach bars, and the mood heats up most between
10 p.m. and midnight
. Some places stay open until 1 or 2 a.m.

You can easily walk the beach and Alona Beach Road. To go beyond the beach, use a tricycle (about
for a short ride) or Grab.
Scooters rent for about
a day, but you need an international driving permit and a helmet, and some shops will deliver to your lodging.
Most tour booths and dive shops are within walking distance of where you stay, so you rarely need a car to book hopping tours or dives.
The best time for Alona Beach is the dry season from
November to May
. The skies are clear and the sea is calm, giving good visibility for snorkeling and diving, and it is comfortable at about
during the day and
at night.
December to April
is peak season, when the beach and restaurants fill up and room rates rise, while
November
is a sweet spot with good weather and fewer people.
June to October
is the wet season with frequent rain, and from
late July to September

the southwest monsoon makes the sea rough, so hopping tours and dives are canceled more often. When the sea on the Alona side is rough, Doljo Beach on the other side of the island is an alternative. There have been reports of jellyfish and sea lice in
April to June
, so check local advice before you get in the water. Just as Typhoon Odette passed over Bohol in
December 2021
, typhoons and tropical depressions from
October to December
can also disrupt flights and fast ferries.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Beachfront resorts let you step straight from your room onto the sand, which makes them popular, and they cost about
or more per night. Hotels and guesthouses on the inner lanes,
5–10 minutes
on foot from the beach, cost about

, and the price gap is not large while the nights are quieter. If the evening music bothers you, choose a room near either end of the beach rather than the middle. Book two or three months ahead for peak season from
December to April
and for holidays.

Food comes in two kinds. Beachfront restaurants offer a wide range of menus, from Filipino to Korean, Italian, Spanish and steak, but prices are higher than the Philippine average, while the local eateries on the inner road are much cheaper. The signature dish is the seafood barbecue you pick from the ice, and be sure to try kinilaw, the Filipino ceviche-style dish (fish cured in vinegar), drinks made with calamansi, and mango shakes. Plenty of shops along the beach sell inexpensive fruit juice and beer, which is great for a midday break.
The best times for photos and walks are before
and just before sunset. From
11 a.m. to 3 p.m.
the ultraviolet rays are strong and the beach is crowded.
At high tide the beach gets narrower, and at low tide the water recedes far out and seaweed is exposed. The hours around high tide are best for swimming.
Prices for hopping tours and massages quoted by touts on the beach are negotiable. First check whether the environmental fee, snorkeling gear and lunch are included.
There are several ATMs around the beach, but they sometimes run out of cash on peak-season weekends. Environmental fees for hopping and small shops often take cash only, so bring plenty.
When you choose seafood at a restaurant, ask the price per weight and the cooking charge beforehand, and check the total after you receive the receipt.
There is little parasol shade at midday, so bring a hat, sunglasses, reef-friendly sunscreen and a rash guard.
When snorkeling, wear water shoes and do not step on coral or seaweed. The sea off the beach has sharp coral in the shallows.
Some restaurants and dive shops can help in Korean, which is useful if your English is limited. For a shop with a Korean instructor, it is easier to book ahead.

The shallow bottom off the beach has sharp coral fragments and sea urchins, and people often get hurt walking barefoot. Wear water shoes when you go in, and watch your footing especially when the water has receded.

Around the beach bars at night, do not leave your phone or wallet on the table, and do not walk alone down dark paths toward the end of the beach late at night. Check the price of drinks and massages offered by touts first.
Agree on the fare in advance for tricycles and taxis. Some drivers at the airport exit quote high fixed fares, so using the Grab fare as your benchmark helps.
Touching or stepping on coral, sea turtles and starfish is prohibited and you can be fined if caught. Do not throw trash on the beach.
During the southwest monsoon from
late July to September
and the typhoon season from
October to December
, hopping tours and dives may be canceled. Do not pack your schedule too tightly, and check the refund rules.

The stretch in front of the beach has changed through erosion-control works and demolitions, and at high tide the sand becomes much narrower. Do not leave your belongings near the water's edge, and check the latest notices for tours and access rules right before you set out.
